candidates.summary: Runway backtest / 'how wrong was our runway number?' scorecard: replay the forecast as of 3, 6 and 9 months ago using only the data available then, compare it with the cash that actually followed, and show the realized error and the P10-P90 band coverage next to today's runway. Where coverage is poor, add a trend-aware band (bootstrap on detrended residuals plus a fitted burn slope).
candidates.hypothesis: The current recentred bootstrap in src/lib/finance/forecast.ts captures month-to-month noise but not trends, which the README itself admits. On companies whose burn drifts (hiring steps, growing AWS/OpenAI spend, revenue growth), its P10-P90 band covers realized 6-month-ahead cash in well under 80% of cases. A trend-aware variant restores coverage to 75-85% without widening the band by more than 1.5x. A visible track record ('our band contained reality 8 times out of 10') is a trust asset that no bank dashboard shows.
candidates.mve: Write a script (scratchpad or src/lib/eval) that generates 200 seeds x 2 noise levels x 3 drift profiles (as generated, +1 hire at month 14, revenue growth halved after month 12) by post-processing generateDemoCompany output. For each company and each cutoff t in {12..20}, run monthlyHistory + computeSnapshot + forecastCash on transactions up to t only, then record whether realized cash at t+3 and t+6 falls inside P10-P90, the signed runway error, and the band width. Report coverage by profile for the current method and for the detrended variant. The idea is falsified as a feature need if the current method's 6-month coverage is already 70-90% on every profile. The fix is falsified if the variant does not raise coverage by 10pp or more at under 1.5x the width.

candidates.summary: Committed vs discretionary burn split and 'survival runway': classify every outflow stream as locked (payroll, rent, insurance, annual contracts until their renewal date), cancellable at next renewal, or discretionary now (monthly SaaS, meals, travel, one-offs). Show the floor burn reachable in 30, 60 and 90 days, the maximum 'survival runway' if everything cuttable were cut, and a dated unlock timeline of when each commitment can be exited.
candidates.hypothesis: Headline net-burn runway hides two numbers founders need when a raise slips: how far runway could stretch, and how fast. On bank data alone, recurring-stream detection, categories and the renewals calendar are enough to classify more than 90% of outflow dollars correctly, and the 90-day survival runway differs from headline runway by at least 2 months for most seed-stage profiles. That makes it a non-trivial number worth showing, and a natural entry point into Copilot cut plans.
candidates.mve: Across 200 seeds x 2 noise levels (plus a variant profile with 2 annual contracts and a lease), run the pipeline and label each outflow stream by rule (category + cadence + next renewal from upcomingRenewals). Score it against generator ground truth derived from DEMO_CATEGORY_LABELS and the SUBSCRIPTIONS table (annualMonth marks annual contracts). Report dollar-weighted classification accuracy, floor burn at 30/60/90 days, and survival-runway minus headline runway. The idea is falsified if dollar-weighted accuracy is below 85% on the noisy feed, or if survival runway exceeds headline runway by under 1 month in more than 70% of companies (nothing worth showing because payroll dominates).
evidence: https://rho.co/blog/discretionary-expense (Rho's own guide: cutting discretionary spend 10% can add about a quarter of runway; a single-vendor benchmark of under 10% discretionary)
https://stealthagents.com/research/startup-burn-rate-benchmarks (attributes 68% payroll share at seed to HSBC; unverified)

candidates.summary: Covenant / bank-minimum breach date: the user enters one or more cash floors (a venture-debt minimum-cash covenant, a bank minimum balance, or a self-set floor such as 3 months of payroll). Runway computes the date at which the probability of crossing each floor passes 10%, 50% and 90% from the existing Monte Carlo paths, alerts on that date instead of on the zero-cash date, and adds it to the Monday digest. A shareable lender-facing compliance snapshot is an optional extra.
candidates.hypothesis: For companies carrying venture debt, the binding constraint is the covenant floor, not zero cash. The existing 'low runway' alert, keyed to zero-cash runway, fires after the covenant has already been breached in a material share of paths. A breach-date alert gives at least 3 months more lead time, which is the window for negotiating a waiver. It also opens a paid tier and a channel: lenders and fractional CFOs who monitor covenants across many companies.
candidates.mve: Generate 200 seeds x 3 burn-drift profiles. Attach a synthetic facility (for example a $1M draw added to cash at month 10 and amortizing monthly debits) with a covenant floor drawn from {20%, 35%, 50%} of the facility. Keep the per-path cash trajectories from forecastCash (add a hook that returns them if they are not exposed) and compute the first month P(cash < floor) >= 0.2. Compare its lead time with the month at which the existing low-runway alert threshold would fire, and with the realized breach month in the generated future. The idea is falsified if the existing alert already precedes the realized breach by 2 months or more in over 90% of companies, or if the breach-date alert has a false-positive rate above 30%.
evidence: https://beancount.io/blog/2026/09/21/venture-debt-vs-equity-warrants-covenants-founder-guide (minimum cash covenant described as the most common tripwire; plan a buffer above it)
https://www.phoenixstrategy.group/blog/venture-debt-for-healthcare-startups-key-tradeoffs (cash at least 35% of facility; 200-300bp step-up on breach; single source)

candidates.summary: 'What has waiting cost us?' cost-of-delay meter and Inbox ordering: for each open finding, compute the cash already lost since it was first detected and the runway-days it costs per week of inaction. Because annual renewals lock in a year of spend, findings whose next renewal date is close carry a cliff, and the Inbox is ordered by cost of delay (monthly $ x urgency to lock-in) rather than by raw $ impact. A digest line reads 'Indecision cost you $X / N runway-days this month'.
candidates.hypothesis: Approval fatigue means founders act on only a few Inbox items per week. Under a fixed approval budget of k items per week, ordering by cost of delay (renewal cliff aware) captures at least 15% more realized savings over 6 months than ordering by monthly $ impact, because it avoids missing annual renewal windows. The visible 'cost of waiting' number gives users a reason to return weekly, so it works as a retention hook.
candidates.mve: On 200 seeds x 2 noise levels (with annual renewal dates randomized via annualMonth), run detectors at a rolling weekly cadence over the last 6 generated months. Simulate a user who approves k in {1,2,3} items per week under three orderings: $ impact, cost of delay, and random. An approved cancel or downgrade stops charges from the next billing date, and a missed annual renewal locks the charge for 12 months. Measure realized savings over the window and the number of renewal windows missed. The idea is falsified if cost-of-delay ordering beats $-impact ordering by under 5% at every k, or if the two orderings agree on more than 90% of picks.
evidence: /home/user/AITX-MLOps-Hack/research_notes/Runway product go to market/retention_features.md (approval fatigue: users approve ~93% of prompts; recommends ranking and batching the Inbox by $ impact)

candidates.summary: Privacy-safe peer benchmark ('how does our spend mix compare with similar startups?') as a growth asset: report spend-category shares (payroll, software, cloud, AI API, rent) and burn multiple as percentiles within a cohort cell (stage x headcount band), built only from opted-in tenants' aggregates with k-anonymity and differentially private noise. Publish a quarterly public 'Startup Spend Index' for acquisition, and show 'you vs peers' inside the app. This covers category mix, not the SKU price benchmarks that Ramp and Vendr own.
candidates.hypothesis: Category-share benchmarks with privacy protection become stable at small cohort sizes: with k >= 25 companies per cell and epsilon = 1 Laplace noise, the reported P25/P50/P75 shares fall within +/-3pp of the true cohort percentiles. A pre-PMF product could therefore publish a credible index with a few hundred opted-in companies. This is a cold-start question no competitor's public report answers. Free burn benchmark pages online are unsourced and conflicting, which leaves room for a transparent one.
candidates.mve: Extend the generator via a wrapper (scale headcount/payroll 0.5-3x, SaaS count, and AI-API share by seed) to produce a synthetic population of 5,000 companies with known category shares. For cohort sizes N in {10,25,50,100,250} and epsilon in {0.5,1,2}, repeatedly sample cohorts, compute DP-noised percentile shares from per-company pipeline output (rules-only categorization on the noisy feed), and measure error against the population truth, including the error from miscategorization. Find the minimum N where the 95th-percentile error is 3pp or less. The idea is falsified as a near-term asset if the required N per cell exceeds 250, or if categorization error alone exceeds 3pp.
